items: Classes & Objects: A class defines state and behaviour; objects are instances of that definition.
Properties & Methods: Class state held in properties, and behaviour implemented as methods.
Static & Constants: Members belonging to the class itself rather than to any one instance.
Traits: A bundle of methods mixed into classes to share behaviour horizontally.
Abstract Classes: A partial base class that forces subclasses to complete certain methods.
Constructor Property Promotion: Declaring constructor parameters as properties in a single step (PHP 8).
Data Mapper: A layer that moves objects to and from storage without the object knowing SQL.
Design Principles: Guidelines such as SOLID that keep object designs flexible.

8233.title: Well, wrong, in fact, you can access properties and methods in a host class
8233.code:
<?php
trait PriceUtilities
{
    public function calculateTax(float $price): float
    {
        // is this good design?
        return (($this->taxrate / 100)  *  $price);
    }

    // other utilities
}
8233.explanation: You might assume that static methods are really the only way to go as far as traits are concerned. Even trait methods that are not declared static are essentially static in nature, right? Well, wrong, in fact, you can access properties and methods in a host class:

8234.title: Here is a host—PriceUtilities—amended to declare the property
8234.code:
<?php
class UtilityService extends Service
{
    use PriceUtilities;

    public $taxrate = 20;
}

    If you think that this is a bad design, you’re right. It’s a spectacularly bad design.
Although it’s useful for the trait to access data set by its host class, there is nothing to
require the UtilityService class to actually provide a $taxrate property. Remember
that traits should be usable across many different classes. What is the guarantee or even
the likelihood that any host classes will declare a $taxrate?
    On the other hand, it would be great to be able to establish a contract that says,
essentially, “If you use this trait, then you must provide it certain resources.”
    In fact, you can achieve exactly this effect. Traits support abstract methods.
